> it’s more like “predict the full output in full for this blob of input text"

Hm. I would actually go so far as to say "predict" is just the wrong word to use in 2026, as it smuggles in an out-of-date picture of what LLMs are that's from the pre RLVR era, and which is frequently used to suggest they don't model anything real in the world but rather the statistics of language, and thus have all sorts of limitations that they've now surpassed ("an LLM will never solve a major open mathematics problem, they're just predicting tokens"). These days I tend to use the more neutral phrase "generate the next token"; I'd only say "predict" in the technical context of (say) the pre-training part of the training run where the object is indeed to minimize the cross-entropy loss function by predicting next tokens in existing text. Generating a token with a modern LLM is better described as something like, "given a context and the weights from the totality of its training, including not just next token prediction with pre-training but also solving vast numbers of math and coding problems with RLVR, the LLM generates tokens one by one." (Consider that an LLM trained purely to optimize for next token prediction with pre-training is terrible at programming and math tasks, as we all remember from 2024. In that sense the amazing results we've seen in the past two years are due to the departure from pure "next token prediction" that RLVR made possible.)

Put another way: would it be useful to describe the AlphaZero chess engine as "just a next move predictor"? (It, too, was a large neural network trained with RL.) I would rather say: "it's playing chess by generating the next move given the state of the board." Which is what humans do too, though we do it with different hardware.

Anyhow. I'm not sure the weight understanding is all that strange. (It's impressive, but so are many thing LLMs do these days.) LLMs are very very good at coding and math problems, of which this is one, and in particular, their RLVR training presumably includes many tasks involving neural networks, doing tasks with PyTorch, etc. It's amazing and impressive, I agree, but I'd say less amazing than proving major open theorems in mathematics, which we already know they can do.

children.author: ninglor

> “breakout game weights” always look the same regardless of training and model

The prompt told Astra what the input and output layers mean -- that is, how the current state of the game is turned into a vector for matrix multiplication, and how the result of those multiplications is turned into an action to take in-game.

Astra saw that the model was trained on a game where the player is at the bottom of the grid and moves left and right, reward objects live at the top, and there's some not-player-controlled thing moving around in the middle. Astra knows that this type of game is called "breakout."

A model that plays breakout will have meaningful weights for the player being in the bottom row, but not for the player being anywhere else, because the player can't go anywhere else. Astra saw that there were meaningful weights for the player in the bottom row, and nodes representing the player in any other row had low-magnitude noise, so the model had never been trained on the player being anywhere besides the bottom row.

Similarly, breakout has "reward" objects in the top rows, and "there is a reward object at [COORDINATE]" is part of the input layer. Astra saw that the model was trained on reward objects in the top few rows.

Here is the code Opus 5.5 is claiming fits a 641-parameter MLP to parity of 8 inputs:

  # Fits small MLPs to 8-bit parity (the full 256-row truth table) with
  # full-batch AdamW, written out in numpy (no PyTorch, so it won't match a
  # PyTorch run bit for bit), and reports for each shape how many of 20 seeds
  # reach 100% accuracy and the median accuracy. Needs Python 3.9+ and numpy.
  import itertools

  import numpy as np

  X = np.array(list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=8)), float)  # all 256 inputs
  y = X.sum(1) % 2


  def nparams(widths: list[int]) -> int:
      """Parameter count of a dense MLP with these layer widths, biases included."""
      return sum(a * b + b for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]))


  def train(
      widths: list[int],
      seed: int,
      steps: int = 4000,
      lr: float = 1e-2,
      wd: float = 1e-4,
  ) -> float:
      """Full-batch AdamW on all 256 inputs; returns the final training accuracy."""
      rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
      P = []    # parameters: W0, b0, W1, b1, ...
      for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]):
          bound = 1 / np.sqrt(a)    # same as PyTorch nn.Linear's default init
          P += [rng.uniform(-bound, bound, (a, b)), rng.uniform(-bound, bound, b)]

      m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam first moments
      v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam second moments
      nlayers = len(widths) - 1
      for step in range(1, steps + 1):
          hs = [X]    # hs[i] is the input to layer i
          zs = []     # pre-activations
          h = X
          for i in range(nlayers):
              z = h @ P[2 * i] + P[2 * i + 1]
              zs.append(z)
              h = np.maximum(z, 0) if i < nlayers - 1 else z    # ReLU; linear output
              hs.append(h)

          logit = h[:, 0]
          prob = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(logit / 2))    # sigmoid without overflow
          g = ((prob - y) / len(y))[:, None]    # d(mean cross-entropy)/d(logit)
          G = [None] * len(P)    # gradients, parallel to P
          for i in reversed(range(nlayers)):
              G[2 * i] = hs[i].T @ g
              G[2 * i + 1] = g.sum(0)
              if i > 0:
                  g = (g @ P[2 * i].T) * (zs[i - 1] > 0)

          # AdamW, using PyTorch's default values for betas (0.9, 0.999) and eps (1e-8)
          for k in range(len(P)):
              P[k] -= lr * wd * P[k]    # decoupled weight decay
              m[k] = 0.9 * m[k] + 0.1 * G[k]
              v[k] = 0.999 * v[k] + 0.001 * G[k] ** 2
              P[k] -= lr * (m[k] / (1 - 0.9 ** step)) / (
                  np.sqrt(v[k] / (1 - 0.999 ** step)) + 1e-8)

      # accuracy of the last forward pass, i.e. before the final update
      return ((logit > 0) == (y > 0.5)).mean()


  for w in [[8, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1], [8, 8, 4, 2, 1], [8, 8, 1], [8, 16, 1], [8, 64, 1]]:
      accs = [train(w, seed) for seed in range(20)]
      print(w, nparams(w), "params; seeds at 100%:", sum(a == 1 for a in accs),
            "/ 20; median acc", np.median(accs))
I might not know enough about ANNs to spot if it's cheating on some way, but it looks legit. It does indeed output that the [8, 64, 1] configuration gets 100% accuracy on all 20 seeds.

It looks like Astra picked the "random task", and the task it picked was 8-bit parity, which is easy to design a circuit for that computes the answer perfectly, but sort of maximally difficult to fit with any kind of gradient descent. It's a great choice for what you asked, which was to find a case where AdamW doesn't come close to the theoretical optimum fit. But I'm less convinced that it tells us much about Astra's capabilities at handcrafting weights in general.

8-bit parity is a^b^c^d^e^f^g^h, which you can compute with minimal depth as ((a^b)^(c^d))^((e^f)^(g^h)). You can compute x^y as x&~y | y&~x. With ReLU activation, i | j is ReLU(i + j): weights of 1, bias of 0. And i & ~j is ReLU(i - j): weights of 1 and -1, still bias of 0. So a two-input XOR is three neurons in two layers, and the tree of 7 binary XORs is 21 neurons in 6 hidden layers. I don't know why Astra needed 433 parameters. Only 42 nonzero parameters are needed. Maybe the other 391 parameters are zeros that the Transformer model demands to be present.

With an RNN you can compute the parity of a string of any length with only three neurons.

Actually, I handed that to Claude Opus 5.5 to check, and it sensibly pointed out that x&~y is mutually exclusive with y&~x, so XOR doesn't even need the third neuron, except in the last layer; you can just fold the addition into the weights of the next layer, which means you only need 4 layers and 15 neurons. But about half of those neurons need 4 nonzero input weights instead of 2, so you still need 42 nonzero weights. It's a good thing you don't need those OR neurons, too, because my definition is wrong: ReLU(1+1) = 2.

Also it explained how to design a 28-parameter net that I don't quite understand, and also a single-hidden-layer network with 8 ReLUs, which I also don't understand, but it needs more parameters: $\text{parity}=s+\sum_{k=1}^{7}2(-1)^k\,\mathrm{ReLU}(s-k)$ where I think $s=\sum_i x_i$.

Somewhat more surprisingly, it also said it didn't have any trouble fitting a 641-parameter network to this problem with AdamW.

I believe we've known humans can handcraft weights much more efficiently than standard gradient descent methods, we just don't have enough memory or time to scale ourselves, so it makes sense to train a neural network to do it on our behalf. I am excited to see how far we can push this method.

Our visual system deals with TB of video input every second but we are able to filter through it and spot the important bits. We can even with closed eyes make our mind spin up visual scenes and alter them. I think that's quite possibly a useful explanation of what's happening here.

The way I interpete it, is vast amounts of text are to LLMs, in some ways like vision is to us. Not seeing tokens, but seeing the "shapes" between them. Like we don't parse pixels but see the whole picture at once.

They triangulate efficiently on the meaning from all the text, instead of rolling it through a lossy feedback system.

It is why they are so good at processing ambiguity. They can combine ambiguity from any parts of the text, near equally well, even on long form text.

But biological brains appear to exhibit the same kind of superposition storage as well, and yet they are very plastic.

It does, one of my ongoing research papers is about it. But I would ask people to take a look at the established idea of Hypernetworks: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.06955v3 Modern version of the field comes from Google Brain around 2016 https://arxiv.org/pdf/1609.09106.

In general my personal research thesis is that current deep learning is much less malleable and neuroplastic as it should be, I got into interpretability because of this. Many focus on safety, but I prioritize it as a toolbox that allows for greater shaping of the underlying intelligence system. If we can fully understand how learning happens, where information is stored and how it is processed, unlike in biological brains, we can apply edits and transformations in digital ones. And if I can use a technique to edit weights based on some underlying reasoning about a system (with a caveat that it leads to something worthwhile), so can an agent. Hence self-improvement. There are many interesting implication to weight space research, and I very much encourage people to read about it. But it is also very easy to overstate what is currently possible, in fact I'd say better to know what is not so one can make it possible.
